title: Rootcause hunt: latency deltas (quick reference)
content:
Purpose:
This is a compact, pragmatic runbook for hunting down small-to-medium latency regressions observed in the serving runtime. The goal is to get from alert -> hypothesis -> repro or mitigation within a 2–6 hour window. Keep this doc pinned in the pager rotation and copy snippets into incident threads.

Scope and when to use it:
- Applies to 95th/99th percentile token generation or end-to-end request latency regressions (hosted + dedicated).
- Intended for regressions that are not obviously caused by infra (node OOMs, networking outage) — those are handled by SRE runbooks.
- Best used when: Grafana SLO panels show an upward step, canary diff shows a delta, or synthetic nightly benchmarks spike.

Quick triage checklist (first 20 minutes):
1) Capture baseline metrics (don’t change anything yet):
   - Open Grafana: Serving latency overview + the canary-vs-prod compare panel. Save a snapshot.
   - Run metrics query for the last 6h and 24h: copy the query results (95p, 99p, p50, error rate, queues).
   - Note the alert rule that fired and its threshold.
2) Confirm signal validity: 
   - Is this global or region-specific? (check region-tagged panels).
   - Any correlated infra alerts? (k8s node changes, GPU node reboots, AZ issues).
   - Check recent deploys: who deployed in the last 4 hours? Link to PRs.
3) Short mitigation (if user-facing SLO at risk):
   - Roll back recent canary or ramp down canary traffic to reduce risk.
   - Route to a lower-cost but stable model variant if cost/latency policy supports it.

Hypothesis matrix (fast form):
- H1: Model or weights change (new ops, different kv size) -> check model catalog + PR history.
- H2: Serving runtime change (kernel selection, caching, batching) -> check commits, feature flags.
- H3: Upstream infra (driver/kernel/GPU firmware) -> check node events and cloud provider notes.
- H4: Traffic pattern shift (longer sequences, more parallel sessions) -> check request histogram distribution.
- H5: Cache/eviction or KV growth causing memory churn -> check KV cache hit rate and GC metrics.
For each hypothesis capture: quick evidence to confirm or refute (metric names, queries, traces).

Useful commands and queries (copy/paste friendly):
- Grafana snapshot: open compare panel -> Share -> Snapshot -> copy link.
- Prometheus examples:
  * 95p latency: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(runtime_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le))
  * request rate by model: sum(rate(runtime_requests_total[5m])) by (model)
  * KV cache hit ratio: sum(runtime_kv_cache_hits_total) / sum(runtime_kv_cache_requests_total)
- Kubernetes quick checks:
  * kubectl -n serving get pods -l app=runtime -o wide
  * kubectl -n serving logs $(kubectl -n serving get pod -l app=runtime -o name | head -n1) -c runtime --since=15m | tail -n 200
- Runtime-level profiling (non-prod or mirrored requests):
  * start a short pprof collection: curl -sS http://$POD:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30 -o profile.pb
  * convert / view: go tool pprof -http=:8080 ./binary profile.pb
- Hotpath microbench harness (local):
  * tools/microbench/run_local_runner --model $MODEL --seq 1024 --concurrency 8 --tokens 2000 --repeat 50
  * Compare wall-time and per-op breakdowns across commits.

Canary vs Prod comparisons (recommended sequence):
1) Time-align traces: pick the same 10-minute window when both canary and prod were receiving similar traffic.
2) Compare percentiles and request-size buckets, not just mean. Look for headroom compression on p99.
3) Identify top ops in pprof flame graphs and map them to code regions (attention kernels, dispatch, IO).
4) If canary is slower: diff build artifacts (libtorch/cu kernels, operator flags, quantization profiles).

Profiling heuristics and what to look for:
- Spikes in CPU sys time vs user time -> likely scheduling/GC or syscalls.
- NVTX / GPU kernels: longer kernel launches but same kernel mix -> driver/firmware or device contention.
- Increased time in encoding/decoding -> tokenization or transport change.
- More time in kv cache lookup -> evidence for cache misses or serialization overhead.

Repro + isolation strategy (1–3 hours):
- Create a narrow repro: same model, same sequence length distribution, single logical request shape. Use the microbench harness and synthetic replay service.
- Mirror production traffic into a dedicated test cluster if available (do not impact prod). If mirrored replay reproduces the delta, you can iterate fast.
- Try binary search across commits: pick a commit known-good (t0) and current commit (tN). Use the microbench harness to benchmark midpoint commit to locate regression window. Keep runs deterministic (fixed RNG seeds, warmup iterations).

Mitigation options (short-term):
- Rollback or pin model runtime to a previous commit (if runtime change suspected).
- Reduce max concurrency or increase batching timeout to avoid head-of-line effects (temporary knob).
- Increase cache capacity or change eviction policy if eviction churn is the cause.

Postmortem data to collect (before closing incident):
- Grafana snapshot(s) and raw Prometheus queries used.
- pprof profile tarball for affected pods + flame graphs.
- Microbench harness results (CSV) for good vs bad commits.
- Exact commit hashes, PR numbers, and container image digests.
- Timeline: first alert -> triage -> mitigation -> root cause -> fix rollout.

Common pitfalls & notes to save time:
- Don’t assume a single metric tells the story. Correlate request size, backend queue length, and kernel-level profiles.
- Canary delta panels can be misleading when traffic composition differs (e.g., canary saw more long-seq requests). Normalize by request shape.
- Watch for noisy background tasks (periodic maintenance jobs) that can bias p99 for short windows.

Investigation template (paste into incident thread):
- Summary (1 line): observed 99p +30% starting 2026-02-14 03:12 UTC in us-west1.
- Scope: affected endpoints, model variants, % traffic.
- Immediate action: ramped down canary from 20% -> 1% (timestamp).
- Evidence collected: Grafana snapshots (links), pprof (file links), microbench CSVs.
- Current hypothesis: runtime commit c0f3a changed kernel dispatch path -> increased attention kernel latency.
- Next steps: run bisect between commits A..B using microbench harness, collect full pprof on candidate commit.

Notes to self / heuristics learned over time:
- Keep a small curated set of microbench configs that mirror the most common prod request shapes — saves hours.
- Always capture the image digest; 'git blame' on a PR is not sufficient for builds with multi-repo changes.
- When in doubt, produce a deterministic synthetic run: less noise than live traffic.

Escalation and owners:
- Primary: eng-serving-runtime on-call.
- Secondary: infra / platform-engineering if node-level anomalies show.
- Contact list: Samira Chen (owner), Marco Ruiz, SRE on-call channel.

Open action items (if this doc used during live incident):
- [ ] Add the microbench config used to the incident artifacts.
- [ ] Attach pprof profile and microbench CSVs to SERV ticket.
- [ ] Link PR that reverts or fixes root cause.

If you add something useful back to this doc, please append a one-line note with date and initials so the next responder can iterate faster.
